text:
Chipped paint was found and repaired, and no structural damage was found, so the defect condition is the chipped paint.

CHIPPED

Arming lever has abnormal resistance, so it is binding or stiff. Ops check found normal operation, which points toward "NON ISSUE"? The question asks for the condition of the part that was reported. Abnormal resistance fits "STIFF".

STIFF

Multiple cautions appeared on the Genesys avionics while passing the 5G tower, and the upper modes kicked off. Everything returned to normal afterward, so the behavior was temporary rather than a hard failure. Candidate labels are WARNING MESSAGE, MULTIPLE IND, MALFUNCTIONED and INTERMITTENT. The "array of cautions" points most directly to MULTIPLE IND.

MULTIPLE IND

Handle difficult to operate, especially after cold soak, describes stiffness, and the fix was adjusting the latch plates. Candidates are STIFF, BINDS, and OUT OF ADJUST. STIFF best fits the reported condition of hard-to-move operation.

STIFF

The left pack temperature kept rising out of control, even after being shut down and restarted at the lowest setting, so the pack overheated. The smell and smoke are effects of that overheating, and the fix was replacing the ACM and heat exchanger. "OVERHEATED" fits better than "UNCONTROLLABLE" or "SMOKE".

OVERHEATED

Before fluid bleeding was done, the crew saw low brake pressure; trapped air is the suspected cause. The best match is "LOW PRESSURE", since the report centers on the observed low brake pressure.

LOW PRESSURE

Chattering was felt in the nose wheel, the unlock light flickered with each thump, and the fix was repacking the nose landing gear. The reported symptom is chattering, and that phrase appears directly in the report.

CHATTERING

The report names the IPC drum as the subject ("ipc drum damaged"), but the root defect is the fractured rear panel of the module 32 front bearing housing. A broken piece of that panel is what damaged the drum, so the condition of the failed part is the fracture.

FRACTURED

Seat 13F reclines into the exit row, and the fix was adjusting its hydrolock, so the part was out of adjustment.

OUT OF ADJUST

The report traces the dirty sock smell to the no.1 engine being over serviced, and 2 quarts of oil were removed. The failed part's condition is therefore over servicing rather than the odor itself.

OVERSERVICED

The report describes a "cabin overpress" ECAM warning that appeared before the door was opened. Testing of the residual pressure controller and both pressure controllers found no faults. The condition reported is the overpressure warning itself, and the tests showed no actual defect behind it, so the best fit is the warning-message label.

WARNING MESSAGE

The emergency exit lights came on because the no smoking switch was set to ON instead of AUTO, which is a crew switch-setting error rather than a part defect. Candidate labels were ILLUMINATED, MISCONFIGURED and CREW ERROR. CREW ERROR fits best because the stated cause is the wrong switch position.

CREW ERROR

Transmission oil pressure read below 1.0 bar at idle, and troubleshooting traced it to a bad pressure transducer rather than to an actual loss of oil pressure. The part failure is therefore an erroneous low reading from the transducer, which matches READS LOW better than LOW PRESSURE.

READS LOW

Hardware of the wrong size (aft screws of insufficient length) points to WRONG PART, IMPROPER PART, or INCORRECT. IMPROPER PART fits hardware that doesn't conform to the IPC.

IMPROPER PART

Chip light came on in flight and a metal particle was found, so the gearbox is shedding metal.

MAKING METAL

The part that was found defective and replaced is the aft waste tank duct, described as cracked. The full LH lav tank and the inoperative lavs were consequences of that failure, not the condition of the replaced part.

CRACKED

The part that failed is the impulse coupling's pawl rivets, which sheared off. That shearing is what trapped the pawls and destroyed the magneto, so the root condition is the shear.

SHEARED

Oil quantity on the right engine read 9, so the engine was serviced. That points to low oil quantity rather than an underservicing finding.

LOW QUANTITY

Candidates are HOT, OVERHEATED and WARNING LIGHT. The report describes a "batt hot" warning light coming on, but nothing shows the battery was actually confirmed hot. So the condition is the warning light illuminating.

WARNING LIGHT

The part that failed is the CVFDR, which was putting a constant drain on the battery. The battery itself drained only because of this. The closest fitting label for a component drawing current when it shouldn't is SHORTED. Other candidates such as FAULTY, DEPLETED or MALFUNCTIONED are possible, but SHORTED best describes the parasitic drain.

SHORTED

Flap handle overshoot caused a disagree, and the flaps ran normally afterward. That points to a crew or handling issue rather than a part failure. The candidate labels are PILOT ERROR and CREW ERROR; "overshoot" means the handle was moved past the detent.

CREW ERROR

Cover flap found loose → LOOSE

LOOSE

A frame flange with a mis-drilled hole points to a manufacturing or repair drilling error, which fits MISMANUFACTURED best.

MISMANUFACTURED

The part that actually failed is the floor connector wire, which maintenance found broken and then repaired. The light not turning on was only the symptom, so the label describes the wire's condition.

BROKEN

Bearing rotating in the hinge plate means it is no longer held tight in its bore, so the condition is LOOSE.

LOOSE

Door hard to open and close, fixed by lubrication. Candidates are STIFF, BINDS and LACK OF LUBE. The fix was lubricating the latch and tracks, but the reported condition is the door being hard to operate, so STIFF fits best.

STIFF

The report describes smoke or a burning odor in the cockpit when the APU bleed was selected. Inspection found nothing, and a decontamination was performed. Smoke and odor both appear, but smoke is the stronger reported condition and is the usual classification for this kind of event.

SMOKE

Door does not close... options: "INOPERATIVE", "MALFUNCTIONED", "OPEN". A door that won't close suggests "OPEN" or "FAILED". I'd choose MALFUNCTIONED.

MALFUNCTIONED

Inspection was requested; door and girt arm function checked OK, so no defect was found.

NON ISSUE

The door's top lock intermittently sticks closed and has to be freed by hand, and the fix was lubrication. That points to sticking rather than a permanent jam. "STICKING" best describes an intermittent sticking condition.

STICKING

Life vest seal opened... the vest's package seal was found opened, which points to OPEN.

OPEN

The report describes the seat 3B emergency exit path lighting as "burned," which for a light means the lamp has burned out.

BURNED OUT

Reported misaligned and sticky; on inspection the alignment was good and the girt bar was only cleaned. "Dirty" fits the cleaning, but "Sticking" captures the reported condition better.

STICKING

Girt bar slider not engaging the floor fitting; the fix was an adjustment per AMM, so the condition is a part needing adjustment.

OUT OF ADJUST

The left engine only reached 88% N1 during the takeoff roll and did not make full takeoff power. It did make power with the EECs off, which suggests an EEC-related issue, and the item was deferred under the MEL. The part condition here is failure to produce power, so "POWER LOSS" fits better than "MALFUNCTIONED".

POWER LOSS

Damper cylinder found at 0 psi points to lost pressure rather than a visible leak, so PRESSURE LOSS fits over LOW PRESSURE.

PRESSURE LOSS

The report says the flap/slat electronics unit (FSEU) 2 was "faulting" during the BITE check. That unit was removed and replaced, which fixed the flap disagree problem. The condition of the failed part is therefore best described as faulted.

FAULTED

Seat 11F is in the emergency exit row, where seats must not recline, yet it was found reclining. The fix was to lock out the recline. The recline lock was not functioning, so the best fit is UNLOCKED.

UNLOCKED

This looks like an escape slide/raft pack at the bottom of the R1 door with excess material protruding, which was repacked. The closest label is IMPROPER STOW, though UNPACKED is a possible alternative.

IMPROPER STOW

Paint was found scrapped/chipped; label CHIPPED.

CHIPPED

The report describes a compressor stall with a loud bang, heavy vibration and an ITT exceedance, followed by an in-flight shutdown and engine replacement. Candidate labels are STALLED, SHUTDOWN and OVERTEMP. The report title names the failure as a compressor stall, so STALLED is the best fit for the condition of the part.

STALLED

Existing repair found not in conformity due to incorrect fasteners — this is a prior repair done wrong.

MISREPAIRED

Reported as "indicator light inop or damaged," but the fix was cleaning debris and excess girt bar lube, and troubleshooting found no trouble. The light did not work as reported, so the reported condition is inoperative. Contamination is a possible alternative, but the report frames the failure as the light being inop.

INOPERATIVE

The defect is that the wrong bulbs were installed in the light assembly. They were replaced with the proper 368 bulbs, which points to WRONG PART rather than INOPERATIVE or IMPROPER PART. WRONG PART is the closer fit.

WRONG PART

Door light illuminated on the takeoff roll and the takeoff was rejected. Troubleshooting found no fault, which points to a light or indication issue rather than a confirmed door problem. The closest labels are FALSE INDICATION, WARNING LIGHT and ILLUMINATED. Since the light came on but the door was not actually unlatched, WARNING LIGHT fits best.

WARNING LIGHT

The report opens with an IDG 1 caution message that led the crew to run the QRH. Candidate labels are WARNING MESSAGE, FAULT MESSAGE and DISCONNECTED. The disconnect was a deliberate crew action per the QRH, not the defect itself, so the discrepancy is the caution message. A caution is closest to WARNING MESSAGE.

WARNING MESSAGE

Emergency lights came on in flight while the switch was in the arm position, meaning they activated without a real need. ACTIVATED would describe this, but the light module itself turned on improperly, so the failure is better described as the module malfunctioning.

MALFUNCTIONED

Spongy brake pedal that goes to the floor, fixed by bleeding — air in the brake system.

AERATED

The best fit is UNLOCKED. The main cargo door light illuminated, the vent windows were found open, and the "door not locked" light was on. Cycling the door showed no defect, so the reported condition is the door being unlocked.

UNLOCKED

The door failed to open normally and needed force, and the fix was re-rigging the hinge and rub blocks. That points to a rigging problem, so the best label is OUT OF RIG. MISRIGGED was considered, but it implies a maintenance error, which the report doesn't indicate.

OUT OF RIG

Shattered windscreen... arcing then shattered. The condition of the failed part: the windscreen shattered, which is closest to CRACKED. Arcing came first, which points to ARCED, but the end condition of the windscreen was shattering, so CRACKED fits better.

CRACKED

Brakes chattering, and air was found in the hydraulic system and bled out. The report describes the reported condition as chattering, so the matching label is CHATTERING.

CHATTERING

Tail strike damage to the fuselage skin, repaired under an engineering repair authorization; DAMAGED is the closest condition label.

DAMAGED

Door damper blown, disc ruptured, shear pin sheared. Candidate labels: RUPTURED, BLEW OUT, SHEARED. The primary condition is the dampener being "blow" (blown), with the disc ruptured, so RUPTURED fits best.

RUPTURED

The report says existing repairs on three frames prevented following the work instructions, so an engineering repair authorization was used instead. No defect was reported for the part itself; the finding was the prior repairs. That fits DISCOVERED better than NON ISSUE.

DISCOVERED

Exit sign fell off and was resecured, so the part came loose from its mounting. The choice is between DETACHED and UNSECURE; "fallen off" describes a part that came free, which fits DETACHED best.

DETACHED

Floor panel with pulled fibers in the corners suggests delamination or damage. "Pulled fibers" is likely composite fraying, but the closest label is probably DELAMINATED or DAMAGED. I'll go with DAMAGED.

DAMAGED

Display picture was stretched and shifting, which is a display malfunction. "Received bad from supply" suggests the part was unserviceable, so the choice is between FAULTY, MALFUNCTIONED and UNSERVICEABLE. MALFUNCTIONED fits the reported symptom best.

MALFUNCTIONED

The girt bar was stuck in its clip because it was not seated on the milled section, so the primary condition is that it was stuck.

STUCK

The report centers on the diversion for a "dirty sock" smell. The cause traced to that smell was a bird strike on the number 1 engine, and the corrective actions (borescope inspection, gaspath wash) address bird ingestion.

BIRD INGESTION fits the identified cause. ODOR would describe only the symptom.

The part condition classification would likely be BIRD INGESTION.

BIRD INGESTION

The life raft stowage came open and could not be stowed again, so DID NOT STOW is the closest fit.

DID NOT STOW

Engine vibration indication spiked; the fix was replacing the accelerometer, so the indication was likely false. Candidate labels are "VIBRATES", "ABNORMAL" and "FALSE INDICATION". The part that failed is the accelerometer, a sensor, which points to a faulty reading. The report states no fault mode beyond the vibration "spiking into abnormal range", so "ABNORMAL" fits that wording, but "FALSE INDICATION" may better describe a failed sensor. Since the report never confirms the reading was false, I'll go with the report's own wording.

ABNORMAL

Drilling the bracket without proper edge distance is a manufacturing error.

MISMANUFACTURED

Options: LOW PRESSURE, EMPTY, PRESSURE LOSS. The report says the slide pressure was "indicating empty," so EMPTY is the closest match.

EMPTY

The failure described is the hydraulic reservoir head pressure dropping to zero and failing to hold. The leak test found no leakage, so LEAKING does not fit. The condition is best described as a loss of pressure.

PRESSURE LOSS

Slide hitting the fuselage when the door opens points to contact between parts.

INTERFERENCE

Emergency light inoperative; fixed by reconnecting the connector. The reported failure condition is that the light did not work, and the reconnect fix points to a disconnected connector. The report's stated condition is "inoperative," so that is the label.

INOPERATIVE

Slide light inoperative; debris found and removed, after which the light worked. The reported condition is the light being inoperative.

INOPERATIVE

Slide found hanging down and incorrectly packed in its housing, so the condition is an improper stow.

IMPROPER STOW

The flight attendant flashlight was reported inoperative. The fix was to reseat it onto its charging pins, which points to "NOT SEATED", but the report itself states the condition as inoperative.

INOPERATIVE

This report describes routine work rather than a failed part: safety pins were installed per the FOM, then removed and stowed, and the door was returned to normal operation. No defect is noted. The closest label is likely DEACTIVATED, since installing the safety pins deactivates the door's emergency systems. NON ISSUE was the other option considered.

DEACTIVATED

This is a chip light indication on the #1 engine. The detectors and plugs were cleaned and reinstalled, and the ops check was good, so there is no confirmed metal. The best fit is the warning light itself.

WARNING LIGHT

Tail strike found during inspection — the part condition is most likely damage from the strike.

DAMAGED

The part that failed is the air cycle machine, and the report says it "seized." That condition is best matched by STUCK, since FROZEN could be confused with icing. The smoke was a symptom of the failure, not the condition of the part, so SMOKE is not the right label.

STUCK

Girt bar cord sticking out of the door, repositioned → OUT OF POSITION.

OUT OF POSITION

Of the offered labels, the report's "disbond" of the horizontal stabilizer skins matches DEBONDED best.

DEBONDED

Slide unravelled off board — the condition is that the slide came unpacked. The safety pin would not lock, but the key event is the slide unravelling, so UNPACKED fits best.

UNPACKED

The failed part is the number 4 wheel hubcap cover. All three of its bolts were found loose with more than 1/4 inch of play. That looseness caused the brake vibration, and the fix was to torque the bolts and safety-wire them. The condition of the part is therefore loose.

LOOSE

Slide visible beneath its cover means the slide pack had shifted out of its stowed position, so this is an improper stow. "Not grounded" in the report refers to the aircraft's status, not an electrical condition.

IMPROPER STOW

Servicing the door damper and emergency operation cylinder cleared the fault, which indicates the cylinder was low on pressure.

LOW PRESSURE

The part is the oven heating element. Maintenance found it was a "bad burning element," meaning the element itself was burning and gave off the fumes. That points to BURNED rather than a general failure or just the fumes symptom.

BURNED

Report mentions odor, fumes, and vapor; the primary complaint is a chemical fume odor with visible vapor. Options are FUMES, ODOR, and VAPOR, with FUMES chosen as the best fit for "chemical fume odor."

FUMES

Vibration indication fluctuating up and down → OSCILLATES? Alternatively ERRATIC. "Goes up and down" fits OSCILLATES or ERRATIC; ERRATIC is more commonly used for indications that fluctuate.

ERRATIC

The girt is the fabric apron attaching the escape slide to the door sill. A "drags" finding with the remedy "repacked" means the girt was out of position, not fully stowed. The strongest fit for a girt hanging down or dragging is IMPROPER STOW, with DRAGGING as the alternative.

IMPROPER STOW

The root cause found was the APU oil level above the full line, with oil overflowing out of the fill port. That points to the oil having been overfilled rather than any part failure.

OVERSERVICED

Debris was found in the aft entry door's exterior handle recess and caused the door light, so the failure condition is foreign object debris.

FOD

The root cause is the sign being connected to the wrong wiring, which makes this a wiring error rather than a failed light.

MISWIRED

Excess girt fabric showing made the slide girt bar hard to arm. The fix was repacking the extra girt material, so the defective condition is the slide pack itself. Candidates are WILL NOT ARM and IMPROPER STOW; the report says "difficult to arm" rather than unable, and the underlying problem was improperly stowed fabric.

IMPROPER STOW

Slide appears to be falling out of its stowed position; options are DISLODGED, IMPROPER STOW, or OUT OF POSITION. The fix was to remove, adjust and reinstall the slide, which points to a stowage issue rather than displacement or damage.

IMPROPER STOW

Reskinning a cargo door usually means the skin was damaged or corroded, but the report gives no cause. Replacing a skin per an SRM repair implies a defect without saying which one, so the general label fits best.

DAMAGED

Door came off its rail, which points to OFF TRACK.

OFF TRACK

Choosing between BLOCKED and OBSTRUCTED for an insect found in the pitot probe: BLOCKED is the more common label for a pitot probe blocked by an insect, so I'm going with that.

BLOCKED

Door 4R would not arm because the girt material had come unpacked around the girt bar, so the failed part's condition is unpacked; "WILL NOT ARM" is only the symptom.

UNPACKED

Flashlight battery needed replacement, so it was depleted. Candidates are DEPLETED, WEAK and LOW. DEPLETED fits a dead battery best.

DEPLETED

Debris in the girt bar was found as the cause of the arming problem. The reported symptom is that the door will not arm, but the label should reflect the part's condition, so FOD fits best.

FOD

This report is routine maintenance documentation. It records the L2 door emergency control handle safety pin being installed for the scheduled door slide R&R, then removed afterward per the AMM and the RII requirements. No part is described as failed, malfunctioning or defective, so the best fit is NON ISSUE.

NON ISSUE

The copilot primary flight display failed, and troubleshooting found it "distorted." DISTORTED is on the list and matches the described condition.

DISTORTED

Washers were mounted on the valve that the CMM says must not be fitted, so the condition is a part installed incorrectly.

MISINSTALLED

Light does not push to test; the fix was reseating the switch. The condition is best captured as the light failing to work.

INOPERATIVE

Shimming the strike plate restored proper latch contact, so the condition is a fit or adjustment problem rather than a damaged part. The closest label for that is "OUT OF ADJUST".

OUT OF ADJUST

The latch fails to reach the strike plate, and shims were added to restore contact. That points to a rigging or adjustment gap rather than a broken or worn part, so the closest fit is "OUT OF ADJUST" (alternatives considered: MISALIGNED, OUT OF RIG).

OUT OF ADJUST

The jo-bolts in the service door inner skin were "not properly installed," and the oversized holes point to an installation fault rather than wear or damage.

MISINSTALLED

Wires had pulled loose from the connectors, so the failed part's condition is best described as backed out, given the repinning fix. The "pulled loose" wording could also suggest PULLED or DISCONNECTED, but repinning points to pins that backed out.

BACKED OUT

Both main gear doors stayed open after gear retraction. Tech support suspects the doors were slow to close. The candidate labels are OPEN and SLOW; OPEN describes the condition the crew observed, so it fits best.

OPEN

Door hard to arm/disarm; fixed by re-adjusting the girt bar position and lanyard straps, so the part was out of adjustment. "STIFF" was considered, but the corrective action points to OUT OF ADJUST.

OUT OF ADJUST

The slide was physically dragging on the door threshold, and the fix was resecuring the velcro. That suggests the slide pack was displaced or unsecured, but the observed condition stated in the report is the dragging itself.

DRAGGING

Handle won't move; latch pin had buildup and was fixed by cleaning and lubing. That points to a lubrication issue, though STUCK and DIRTY were also candidates. The "excessive build up" suggests dirt, but the corrective action was clean-and-lube, and the symptom is that the handle is stuck, so LACK OF LUBE fits best.

LACK OF LUBE

The failed part is the L2 door lower forward and aft latch receivers. They were found "out of clearance" and had to be adjusted, so the condition is an adjustment problem rather than an electrical or indication fault.

OUT OF ADJUST

Bottle at 0 psi, serviced to 1500 psi. The best fit is either "DEPLETED" or "LOW PRESSURE". Zero pressure is better described as DEPLETED.

DEPLETED

Over pressure in the gauge points to the OVERPRESSURED label.

OVERPRESSURED

Girt hanging too low and re-secured suggests UNSECURE or OUT OF POSITION. "Re-secured" points to UNSECURE.

UNSECURE

Flaps stopped at flaps 2 and the gauge disagreed with the commanded position, but the BITE found no faults and the ops test was normal. That points to an intermittent fault rather than a confirmed part failure. The gauge mismatch alone could suggest a false indication, but the flaps physically failing to retract also points to intermittent.

INTERMITTENT

Megaphone voice output was very low and barely audible, and replacing the batteries fixed it, so the condition is weak output.

WEAK

Panel partially departed in flight → INFLT SEPARATION. Cause: fasteners not properly installed, which would point to MISINSTALLED. The condition of the part is that it departed, so INFLT SEPARATION fits best.

INFLT SEPARATION

Inspection found the slide pack inflation cylinder pressure good per the AMM, so the reported overpressure was not a real defect.

NON ISSUE

Flaps locked by the wing tip brake, and the unit removed is described as faulted. The label could be LOCKED or FAULTED. The part condition is the flaps being locked, so LOCKED fits best.

LOCKED

Existing repair found without records — repair installed without documentation. Candidates: MISREPAIRED, DISCOVERED, INSTALLED. "Found installed without records" fits INSTALLED or DISCOVERED. INSTALLED is the closest match to the wording, so I'll go with that.

INSTALLED

Flap lockout caused by an invalid skew sensor reading; the FSEU and sensors were replaced. The condition is best described as a fault. Options considered were "FAULTED", "INOPERATIVE" and "MALFUNCTIONED". The flap lockout itself is a malfunction, and a lockout is typically a fault condition, so "FAULTED" fits best.

FAULTED

Maintenance traced the reported oil leak to a pinhole in the scavenge pump housing caused by cavitation erosion through the pump body. The leak is the symptom; the defective condition of the part is erosion.

ERODED

Of the candidate labels, "UNPACKED" fits better than "UNLACED" or "IMPROPER STOW" because the slide was unraveling and its z-fold had come undone.

UNPACKED

Prox switch required adjustment, so OUT OF ADJUST fits.

OUT OF ADJUST

Lavs were serviced and all operate normally, so no defect was found.

NON ISSUE

Excess girt material on the door 2R slide is not caught against the retainers and not tucked as the AMM requires, so the slide is improperly stowed.

IMPROPER STOW

Door would not close properly; the fix was replacing the lower latch pushrod and then adjusting it per the AMM. That points to the pushrod being out of adjustment. Other candidates: "MALFUNCTIONED" or "FAULTY". "OUT OF ADJUST" seems to fit the fix best.

OUT OF ADJUST

The report says the slide was drooping, which made the bustle protrude. That means the part had moved out of its proper place. The closest fitting labels are DISPLACED and OUT OF POSITION, and "drooping" fits DISPLACED best.

DISPLACED

The report says the CVFDR (cockpit voice and flight data recorder) was causing a constant drain on the aircraft battery. That points to an internal electrical fault, but no specific mode such as a short is confirmed. The general label FAULTY fits best.

FAULTY

Several conditions are reported, but the part condition is the overheat. "Wing overheat" in particular points to a bleed duct overheat, so OVERHEATED fits better than FUMES.

OVERHEATED

The flaps locked out at 9 degrees and a disagree light came on, but all indications were normal once the flaps were driven to 15. Replacing the right flap position transmitter fixed it, which points to that transmitter giving a false disagree signal.

FALSE INDICATION

Low pressure in a door assist bottle could be labelled LOW, LOW PRESSURE or UNDERSERVICED. The report says only "low" and the fix was servicing, so LOW matches the reported condition most directly.

LOW

Wires improperly connected → MISWIRED? Or DISCONNECTED? "Improperly connected" suggests miswired.

MISWIRED

Door rubbing on the threshold plate fits INTERFERENCE.

INTERFERENCE

Lack of lubrication is the direct cause, since lubing the pins fixed it. But the reported condition is that the handle needs abnormally high force to move, which describes a part that is stiff. Choosing between STIFF and LACK OF LUBE, the observed condition fits STIFF better.

STIFF

The nose gear would not retract because a downlock pin had been left installed in the nose landing gear. The defective condition is the pin being installed when it should not have been.

INSTALLED

Door handle was difficult to operate, so the latch is binding or stiff. "BINDS" fits a mechanism that is hard to turn better than "STIFF".

BINDS

Root cause: the sign was connected to the wrong wiring, i.e. miswired.

MISWIRED

Door was hard to disarm, and the fix was cleaning debris from the girt bar attachment points. Candidates are STIFF, BINDS, CONTAMINATED and DIRTY. The report describes how the door behaved ("hard to disarm"), which best matches STIFF.

STIFF

The probable cause stated in the report is "disengagement of the nlg actuator's internal lock," so the condition is DISENGAGED.

DISENGAGED

The report says the right engine failed during takeoff, and metal was found in the 2.5 bleed ports, so the engine was internally damaged. Possible labels are FAILED, MAKING METAL, and DAMAGED. The condition the crew experienced, and the reason for discontinuing takeoff, was engine failure, so FAILED fits best.

FAILED

Transit light stays on, sensor replaced. The part is the position sensor, and it gave a false indication.

FALSE INDICATION

Power turbine second stage blades liberated → label as the part condition. Options are SEPARATED, BROKEN, FRACTURED or DISINTEGRATED. "Liberated" blades are most commonly coded as SEPARATED.

SEPARATED

Ice was removed to fix the door, so the cause is icing. Of "STUCK", "FROZEN" and "ICED", "ICED" names the ice condition most directly.

ICED

The door sticks to the frame and won't freefall when opened. The fix was re-rigging the door hinge, which points to an out-of-rig condition. Still, the reported condition is the door sticking, and the label list offers both STICKS and STICKING to describe it. The fix suggests OUT OF RIG, but the label should describe the discrepancy as reported, so I'll go with STICKS.

STICKS

Key phrase: "yd 2 inop multiple times" — the yaw damper went inoperative repeatedly. The best-fitting label for that condition is INOPERATIVE.

INOPERATIVE

Slide deployed — likely an unintended deployment. The options are DEPLOYED or UNWANTED DEPLOY. The report doesn't state the deployment was inadvertent, so the plain label DEPLOYED fits best.

DEPLOYED

The door actuator failed to raise the door and would not respond to either the inside or outside switch, so the part was inoperative.

INOPERATIVE

The report describes the right hydraulic quantity dropping to 0.73 after engine start. Maintenance serviced the system and found no leaks, so the defect recorded is the quantity reading. That fits "LOW QUANTITY" better than "LEAKING."

LOW QUANTITY

Lavatory oxygen mask door open — mask likely dropped/deployed. Options are OPEN, UNWANTED DEPLOY, UNLATCHED. The door simply opened, and the corrective action was to repack it. The reported condition is the door being open, so I'll go with OPEN.

OPEN

Slide hitting the fuselage suggests interference.

INTERFERENCE

The report describes a loud squeal from the first officer's windshield, which points to a pressurization air leak at the windshield seal. The fix was to retorque both windshields, after which the pressure control ops check and the leak check were good. That fix suggests the windshield fasteners were under-torqued, and LOW TORQUE fits that condition. The other candidates were NOISE and LEAKING, but the corrective action points to the torque.

LOW TORQUE

Under the static discharger base on the rudder, four holes on the LH side and one on the RH side were found "out of standard," meaning they did not meet dimensional requirements, likely through elongation or oversizing. The closest available label for a part that fails to meet its specified dimensions is OUT OF TOLERANCE.

OUT OF TOLERANCE

The report traces the fumes to the #2 engine being over serviced by 2 quarts of oil; the measured oil consumption was within limits. That over-servicing is the defective condition found.

OVERSERVICED

The door 3L slide was not showing armed, and the fix was replacing the door proximity switch. That points to an indication problem: the slide likely was armed but the switch gave no armed indication. "WILL NOT ARM" is possible, but the slide wasn't necessarily unable to arm. "FALSE INDICATION" also fits a faulty proximity switch, and "NO INDICATION" is another candidate. Because the report says the slide was "not showing armed," the indication was false rather than absent, so FALSE INDICATION is the best fit.

FALSE INDICATION

The report says the damaged skin area showed "oil canning", which matches the CANNING label.

CANNING

The part that failed is the trim on top of the lavatory door, and the report verifies it is broken. The sticking door is the symptom, not the condition of the failed part.

BROKEN

The failed part is the ACM (air cycle machine), which was grinding and producing an odor. The pack overheat and the cabin smoke are symptoms of that failure. The candidate labels are OVERHEATED, ODOR, SMOKE and NOISY. The report centers on the odor event (type 6, level b, followed by decontamination), and it names the ACM as making the odor. So the best fit is ODOR.

ODOR

Floor panel upper skin with "pulled strands" means the composite fibers are being pulled loose from the surface. Of the available labels, FRAYED fits this best, ahead of PULLED or DAMAGED.

FRAYED

The hose was found leaking, but the root cause is the elbow missing from the bottom of the acoustic filter. That absence forced the sharp bend in the hose, and the bend caused the leak. Since the condition of the part at fault is its absence, the best fit is MISSING rather than LEAKING.

MISSING

Center tank quantity is on MEL and should be blank, but it displayed a value. That points to a false indication, and the fix was replacing the bussing plug.

FALSE INDICATION

The report says the EPSU failed, and that the failure was caused by a short in the L1 slide harness. The label should describe the condition of the part, and that condition is the short.

The list offers both "SHORT" and "SHORTED". "SHORTED" is the past-tense condition form, matching how the report describes the failure.

SHORTED

Girt bar stowed incorrectly → could be JAMMED or IMPROPER STOW. The resolution shows the root cause was improper stowing, which makes IMPROPER STOW the better fit.

IMPROPER STOW

Lever doesn't move fully, hard to disarm — this most likely points to binding or stiffness. "BINDS" or "STIFF" are the candidates; "STIFF" is the closest match to "hard to disarm."

STIFF

Lights that fail to stay illuminated are not working as intended. INOPERATIVE or INTERMITTENT could fit, but the report gives no sign of intermittency, so the broader label FAILED fits best.

FAILED

The part that failed is the aft sill drain, and the report says it was "clogged with coffee grounds." The odor was only the symptom; the drain's condition is clogged.

CLOGGED

The battery's next due date falls within 90 days, so it is near expiry rather than already expired. That points to "OUT OF DATE" or "EXPIRED". Since it is approaching its due date and has not lapsed, "OUT OF DATE" fits best.

OUT OF DATE

Trouble removing the girt bar from its brackets suggests it is binding or sticking. The fix was cleaning and lubrication, which points to the girt bar being stiff or sticking in the retainer clips. "BINDS" and "STICKING" are both candidates; I chose "STICKING".

STICKING

Chip detector found one flake of metal, within acceptable limits, so the reported indication is not a defect and WITHIN LIMITS fits better than MAKING METAL.

WITHIN LIMITS

Repair done by an MRO without approved data, producing a shaft missing its oil holes, points to a misrepair.

MISREPAIRED

Only one of the R2 evacuation lights was working, so the reported condition is that the light did not operate. Cleaning the electrical connections fixed it.

INOPERATIVE

The aft right-hand door emergency accumulator read 1350 psi at 50°F and had to be serviced up to 1700 psi. The part's condition is therefore low pressure.

LOW PRESSURE

Ten filters from stock all failed to fit the filter boss, which points to a manufacturing defect rather than an installation mistake.

MISMANUFACTURED

The O2 mask at seat 10E was found deployed while passengers deplaned, with no indication it was meant to drop. That points to UNWANTED DEPLOY rather than plain DEPLOYED.

UNWANTED DEPLOY

Annunciator illuminated in flight, but no fault was found on the ground and no maintenance action was required. The report centers on the annunciator lighting up, which fits WARNING LIGHT more closely than ILLUMINATED or FALSE INDICATION.

WARNING LIGHT

Crew heard loud cracking/popping sounds on approach, but the post-flight inspection found nothing wrong. The reported condition is the sound itself, so the closest label is NOISE.

NOISE

The part that failed is the circuit breaker, which was found open. A tripped circuit breaker is usually labeled TRIPPED, and that term fits a breaker that popped open better than OPEN or POPPED do.

TRIPPED

Excess fabric falling out of the slide pack means the slide was not packed or stowed correctly, which fits "IMPROPER STOW" better than "UNPACKED".

IMPROPER STOW

Gear showed not up and locked; the prox sensor was replaced. That points to a false indication from the sensor.

FALSE INDICATION

Both "inoperative" and "stuck" appear in the report. "Stuck in" is the more specific description of the knuckle knocker's condition, so I chose it over "inoperative."

STUCK

This report describes a fuel imbalance that kept returning after the crew balanced it, with the right side running low, plus a totalizer discrepancy. That points to a likely fuel leak on the right side. The best fit is LEAKING, though UNBALANCED is a possible alternative.

LEAKING

Misdrilled is a manufacturing or installation defect. With no repair history mentioned, the closest label is MISMANUFACTURED.

MISMANUFACTURED

Slide needed repacking and was repositioned in its container, which points to an improper stow.

IMPROPER STOW

Slide arm lever "difficult to use" — STIFF fits best.

STIFF

The part that failed is relay K528, and it was found with its socket melted. Melting from heat fits "BURNED" better than "OVERHEATED", since the damage shows the relay actually burned rather than just running hot.

BURNED

The latch made the door hard to open, which points to the latch sticking or binding. "STICKING" fits a latch that resists opening better than "BINDS".

STICKING

Left-hand upper deck emergency door assist bottle reads zero pressure, so the bottle has lost its charge. The closest options are LOW PRESSURE, DISCHARGED, DEPLETED and EMPTY. LOW PRESSURE best fits a pressure gauge reading of zero.

LOW PRESSURE

The failure is defined by the EICAS message ("brake degraded") that appeared, and the part that was replaced was the brake control unit.

WARNING MESSAGE

Choosing a label: the slide arm light failed to illuminate because a green cord was caught in the girt bar, which is an obstruction. "WILL NOT ARM" is a candidate, but the report says the arm light would not illuminate, not that the slide could not be armed. The part condition itself is that something was stuck in the girt bar, which points to "OBSTRUCTED".

OBSTRUCTED

Door activated in emergency mode by ground load crew. Options include ACTIVATED or HANDLER ERROR. The condition of the part is that it was activated, which points to ACTIVATED.

ACTIVATED

The report describes the #2 MLG tire failing on takeoff, and the follow-up was a "tire tread loss or tire burst" conditional inspection. Several labels could fit, including BURST, FAILED and BLEW OUT. The mention of a tire burst inspection, together with debris damage to the flaps and panels, points most specifically to a burst tire.

BURST

Handle alignment stripes not aligned, but the solenoid noise and late actuation suggest the door was not latching correctly. MISALIGNED describes the stripes only, and UNLATCHED fits the door's condition better.

UNLATCHED

Wire harness shows evidence of heat — could be OVERHEATED or BURNED. "Evidence of heat" points to OVERHEATED.

OVERHEATED

The autopilot would not disconnect by any method: the yoke disconnect switch, the AP button, CWS, or pulling the circuit breaker. The pilot had to overpower the servos. Possible labels are FAILED, MALFUNCTIONED and UNRESPONSIVE. Since the autopilot did not respond to any disconnect command, UNRESPONSIVE fits best.

UNRESPONSIVE

Difficult to open/close suggests binding.

BINDS

The defect being reported is on the received rotor brake: its attach plate was installed incorrectly, 180 degrees out. The original out-of-tolerance condition only prompted the replacement. Since the part came back in "repaired" status, the incorrect assembly happened during repair, which points to MISREPAIRED rather than MISINSTALLED.

MISREPAIRED

The pressure switch read "true" while the brake was released, so the defect was a false indication.

FALSE INDICATION

Light stays on and won't turn off, so the condition is that it is illuminated.

ILLUMINATED

Girt bar difficult to arm... options: "WILL NOT ARM" vs "STIFF" vs "BINDS". Very difficult to arm — likely STIFF or BINDS. "WILL NOT ARM" implies couldn't. I'd pick BINDS? Hmm. "Difficult to arm" → STIFF seems fitting.

STIFF

Latch not contacting striker, fixed by shimming — out of adjustment/rig.

OUT OF ADJUST

The report says the oven smelled and produced smoke because of poor cleanliness, and the fix was cleaning the oven interior. The underlying condition of the part is that it was dirty, so DIRTY fits better than SMOKE.

DIRTY

Sign needed reattachment → detached / unsecure. "Re-secured" suggests the sign was loose or unsecure, and "needs to be reattached" suggests DETACHED. Of the two, DETACHED fits the stated need to reattach best.

DETACHED

The part that failed is the hydraulic pump connector. The report says it was "damaged and shorting" on both the pump side and the aircraft side. The overheat light and fumes are consequences of that short, so the condition of the connector is best captured as SHORTED.

SHORTED

Captain opened the door while it was armed — a crew error. However, the label should describe the condition of the part itself, which is "door will not move" and "arming lever is stuck." The best fit for that condition is JAMMED.

JAMMED

Oil quantity dropped to 0% during flight, indicating loss of oil. The candidates are LEAKING, OIL CONSUMPTION, LOW QUANTITY and SHUTDOWN. The engine was manually shut down, but that is a consequence rather than the condition. The core issue is oil depleting in flight, which fits OIL CONSUMPTION best.

OIL CONSUMPTION

Light housing fallen off → DETACHED.

DETACHED

Crew noticed an electrical smell, and the inspection found fluid contamination on the right recirc fan check valve plus dusty filters. The reported condition is the smell itself, so the best fit is ODOR.

ODOR

Girt bar getting caught on the door frame suggests INTERFERENCE or UNSECURE. The fix was to resecure the girt bar, which points to UNSECURE as the part's condition.

UNSECURE

The report says the lining on the flight deck escape hatch fell off in flight, and the fix was to reinstall it. That points to the lining coming loose and separating from the hatch. DETACHED fits that better than INFLT SEPARATION, which usually means a part was lost from the aircraft.

DETACHED

Seized ACM is best captured by the label STUCK.

STUCK

The report centres on the heatshield's spot welds failing, which left the heatshield loose on the exhaust pipe. A hole in the pipe resulted, but that is secondary damage. The condition of the failed part is best captured by the welds failing and the shield coming loose.

LOOSE

The slide pack cover fell off the right mid exit door, meaning it came off its mounting. That points to DETACHED rather than LOOSE, since the cover separated completely.

DETACHED

The report says the exit sign lens fell off, meaning it came away from its mounting. That condition is best labeled DETACHED.

DETACHED

The door was closed, yet the screen still showed it as open. That is an indication that does not match the actual condition, so it is a false indication.

FALSE INDICATION

The part replaced was the upper aft latch fitting, which was found worn on its bearing. The displaced seal was a secondary finding that only needed reinstalling.

WORN

The flaps stopped just off the up position when flaps 1 was selected, which forced a no-flap landing. Afterward the flaps operated normally and the faults cleared. The part most clearly "stopped" moving, and that label is in the list.

STOPPED

Door 2 slide appearing to fall out with excess girt material showing indicates the slide pack was shifted or improperly stowed. "IMPROPER STOW" fits this best.

IMPROPER STOW

Surface scratches on the skin map best to SCORED, which covers scratched surfaces.

SCORED

Cable sawing through the pulley bracket means the cable was wearing into the bracket by rubbing contact. The failed part is the bracket, and its condition is best described as worn from contact. "CHAFED" could also fit, but "WORN" is the more typical label for this kind of cable-sawing damage.

WORN

Battery pack "found poor condition" — common classification for poor condition is DETERIORATED.

DETERIORATED

The takeoff was rejected because of a "hot brakes" message. The part written up and deferred under the MEL is the brake temperature monitoring unit, which suggests a false or faulty indication. Candidate labels are FALSE INDICATION, WARNING MESSAGE and HOT. Because the reported condition is the message itself, WARNING MESSAGE fits best.

WARNING MESSAGE

The part that failed is the system 'b' flight control shutoff valve, and the report says it was found bypassing. The low pressure light is only the symptom.

BYPASSING

Debris was found in the captain's pitot tube, which blocked the tube and produced the erroneous airspeed. The part's condition is therefore best labeled as obstructed by debris.

OBSTRUCTED

The seat at 14F is in an emergency exit row, so its recline should be restricted, yet the seatback still reclines. That points to an improper configuration or setup rather than physical damage. The candidate labels are MISCONFIGURED, MISRIGGED and MALFUNCTIONED. Since the seat simply was not set up as recline-restricted, MISCONFIGURED fits best.

MISCONFIGURED

Door was reported difficult to close, but the ops check was normal and no fault was found. The reported symptom is best captured as STIFF.

STIFF

Key details: the lavatory door is stuck half open, the door is off its track, and the track is bent. The bent track is the defective part condition underlying the door being off track and stuck.

The label could be BENT (track condition), OFF TRACK (door), or STUCK. Classification is by the condition of the failed part. The door being off its track is the primary discrepancy, but the defective part is the bent track.

I'll choose BENT.

BENT

The door failed to show armed because something was blocking the girt bar proximity switch, and removing that obstruction fixed it. The defect is the obstruction itself.

OBSTRUCTED

Insulation blanket lodged in the outflow valve seat, keeping it from closing. Options are OBSTRUCTED, FOD, or PRESSURE LOSS. The part that failed is the outflow valve, which was obstructed by the blanket. The report calls it "fod / obstruction", and the valve's condition is best described as OBSTRUCTED.

OBSTRUCTED

Engine rolled back twice and recovered on its own, with power loss events. The fadec fault message points to the EEC, and the transient, recurring nature fits "INTERMITTENT". Other options considered were "POWER LOSS" and "FAULT MESSAGE". The part involved is the EEC; the event was a rollback, i.e. a power loss. Since the condition being classified is the engine's, POWER LOSS fits best.

POWER LOSS

Several labels could fit this report. The crew had a vibration and an engine vibration CAS message, followed by a shutdown. Troubleshooting then found the N2 locked and the N1 turning very rough with grinding. Debris was found on the chip detector and on 2 of the 4 debris monitors in the gearbox.

The debris on the chip detectors points to internal failure, so "MAKING METAL" is the best fit for the part's condition. The alternatives are weaker: "VIBRATES" describes the symptom, and the shutdown was a consequence of the failure.

MAKING METAL

The part that failed is the upper aft bayonet bolt on the door, and the report calls it a "failure." The secondary damage was sheared rivets, but the classification should describe the condition of the primary part. The report gives no specific failure mode for the bolt itself, such as broken or fractured, so the best fit is the generic label.

FAILED

The report describes double-drilled holes at the tailcone stringer splice. That is a manufacturing or repair defect rather than damage from service. A field repair was then accomplished, which fits a part produced incorrectly.

MISMANUFACTURED

Out of nose-down stab trim, and the fix was rerigging the pitch trim, which points to OUT OF RIG.

OUT OF RIG

I'd go with WORN, though DRAGGING and VIBRATES also fit. The defect found was the number 2 brake assembly worn to limit, and it was also dragging when the aircraft was jacked. The rubbing noise and pedal vibration were symptoms; the primary condition of the part was wear to the limit, which caused the dragging.

WORN

Two problems were found: the forward sensor was faulting and the aft sensor S10217 was wired incorrectly. The rewiring correction points to a wiring error as the defect condition, which corresponds to MISWIRED. The forward sensor fault (FAULTED) also fits, but MISWIRED is the more specific finding.

MISWIRED

The yaw trim actuator was the part replaced. During the AP2 portion of the test, the pedal moved but did not return to neutral, so the actuator stuck in position. That points to STUCK. The test failure itself is only the symptom. Other options like FAILED or MALFUNCTIONED would also fit, but STUCK describes the specific condition seen.

STUCK

Door hard to open/close due to insulation interference at the bellcrank. The candidate labels are INTERFERENCE, STIFF and BINDS. Since the repair was to the insulation near the bellcrank, the cause was interference.

INTERFERENCE

Girt bar placed incorrectly on its rest brackets, then repositioned. Options: OUT OF POSITION, IMPROPER STOW, MISINSTALLED. "Placed incorrectly" and "repositioned" point most directly to OUT OF POSITION.

OUT OF POSITION

This report records a door reskin repair but never names the defect that prompted it. With no condition stated, the closest fit is DAMAGED.

DAMAGED

Complete loss of left brake, fixed by replacing the master cylinder. The failed part is the master cylinder, which most likely lost pressure or stopped working. "FAILED" is the broad option, and "INOPERATIVE" also fits. "PRESSURE LOSS" is plausible, but the report gives no mention of a leak, so I'll go with FAILED.

FAILED

Slide fell out of pack — could be UNWANTED DEPLOY, DETACHED, or DISLODGED. "Fell out of slide pack" suggests the slide came out of its packed state, which best matches UNPACKED.

UNPACKED

The report describes a strong smell of smoke or fumes throughout the cabin and flight deck, with no visible smoke mentioned. That points to ODOR rather than SMOKE or FUMES.

ODOR

The report describes an intermittent lavatory smoke ECAM indication with no actual smoke, and maintenance fixed it by replacing the smoke detector. That points to a false indication from the detector. "INTERMITTENT" is also possible, but the core issue is a spurious warning, so the best fit is FALSE INDICATION.

FALSE INDICATION
